title: Electricity
blurb: From Ohm's law to the fuse board in your hallway.

lessons.title: Voltage, current & resistance
lessons.summary: The three quantities behind every circuit, and the one law that ties them together.

cards.title: Electricity is moving charge
cards.text:
A current is a flow of electric charge. In a metal wire it's electrons nudging each other along. Each electron drifts slowly, but the push travels through the wire almost instantly, like water already filling a hose.

By convention, current is drawn flowing from + to −, the opposite way to the electrons. Every circuit diagram uses this convention.

cards.title: The water analogy
cards.text:
Picture a tank feeding a pipe.
• Voltage is the pressure, set by how high the water stands.
• Current is how much water flows per second.
• Resistance is a narrow section of pipe that limits the flow.

More pressure pushes more flow; a narrower pipe allows less. That's the whole idea behind Ohm's law.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><rect class="w" x="42" y="55" width="66" height="83" rx="0"/><path class="s" d="M40 25 V140 H110 V25"/><path class="a" d="M42 55L108 55"/><rect class="w" x="110" y="119" width="70" height="12" rx="0"/><rect class="w" x="180" y="124" width="55" height="2" rx="0"/><rect class="w" x="235" y="119" width="65" height="12" rx="0"/><path class="s" d="M110 118 H180 V123 H235 V118 H300"/><path class="s" d="M110 132 H180 V127 H235 V132 H300"/><path class="r" d="M24 135L24 60"/><path class="r" d="M27.5 67.2L24 60L20.5 67.2"/><path class="r" d="M24 60L24 135"/><path class="r" d="M20.5 127.8L24 135L27.5 127.8"/><path class="a" d="M250 108L295 108"/><path class="a" d="M287.8 111.5L295 108L287.8 104.5"/><path class="a" d="M130 108L170 108"/><path class="a" d="M162.8 111.5L170 108L162.8 104.5"/></g><text class="r" x="78" y="168" text-anchor="middle">height ≈ voltage</text><text class="a" x="220" y="98" text-anchor="middle">flow ≈ current</text><text class="" x="208" y="152" text-anchor="middle">narrow ≈ resistance</text></svg>

cards.title: Ohm's law
cards.text: Voltage (volts, V) equals current (amps, A) times resistance (ohms, Ω). Cover the quantity you want in the triangle and the other two tell you how to get it.
example: 12 V battery across a 4 Ω heater
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><path class="s" d="M110 20 L20 160 H200 Z"/><path class="s" d="M62 95L158 95"/><path class="s" d="M110 95L110 160"/></g><text class="" x="110" y="82" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:34px">V</text><text class="" x="70" y="146" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:34px">I</text><text class="" x="150" y="146" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:34px">R</text><text class="a" x="268" y="62" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:22px">V = I × R</text><text class="a" x="268" y="98" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:22px">I = V ÷ R</text><text class="a" x="268" y="134" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:22px">R = V ÷ I</text></svg>

cards.title: Try it: dim the bulb
cards.text: Change the voltage and the resistance. Watch the current and the power the bulb turns into light and heat.

cards.title: It's the current that hurts
cards.text:
Your body is a resistor too. What matters for safety is how much current passes through it, and which way.
Around 1 mA you feel a tingle. Near 10 mA muscles can lock and you may not be able to let go. From roughly 50–100 mA across the chest, the heart can go into fibrillation.

That's why home RCDs trip at 30 mA: well before the dangerous zone.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><rect class="rz" x="215" y="98" width="85" height="24" rx="2"/><path class="s" d="M20 110L300 110"/><path class="s" d="M40 103L40 117"/><path class="s" d="M120 103L120 117"/><path class="s" d="M170 103L170 117"/><path class="s" d="M250 103L250 117"/><path class="a" d="M170 72L170 102"/></g><text class="" x="40" y="92" text-anchor="middle">feel it</text><text class="" x="115" y="92" text-anchor="middle">can't let go</text><text class="a" x="170" y="64" text-anchor="middle">RCD trips</text><text class="r" x="255" y="92" text-anchor="middle">heart risk</text><text class="" x="40" y="140" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">1 mA</text><text class="" x="120" y="140" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">10 mA</text><text class="a" x="170" y="140" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">30 mA</text><text class="r" x="250" y="140" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">100 mA</text><text class="" x="160" y="172" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">current through the body (log scale)</text></svg>

quiz.q: A 9 V battery drives current through a 450 Ω resistor. What is the current?
quiz.explain: I = V ÷ R = 9 ÷ 450 = 0.02 A, which is 20 mA.

quiz.q: In the water analogy, what plays the role of voltage?
quiz.explain: Voltage is the push, like pressure. Flow is current; pipe narrowness is resistance.

quiz.q: You double the resistance and keep the voltage the same. The current…
quiz.explain: I = V ÷ R. Twice the R with the same V gives half the current.

lessons.title: Circuits at home
lessons.summary: Series vs parallel, power, and what the breakers in your board actually do.

cards.title: Series vs. parallel
cards.text:
In series, components share a single loop. The same current flows through each and the voltage is split between them. One break stops everything, like old Christmas lights.

In parallel, each component has its own path to the supply. Each gets the full voltage and can be switched on or off independently.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><path class="s" d="M20 95 V60 H140 V150 H20 V115"/><path class="s" d="M7 101L33 101"/><path class="s" d="M14 109L26 109"/><circle class="s bgf" cx="60" cy="60" r="11"/><path class="s" d="M53.2 53.2L66.8 66.8"/><path class="s" d="M66.8 53.2L53.2 66.8"/><circle class="s bgf" cx="100" cy="60" r="11"/><path class="s" d="M93.2 53.2L106.8 66.8"/><path class="s" d="M106.8 53.2L93.2 66.8"/><path class="s" d="M180 95 V60 H300 V150 H180 V115"/><path class="s" d="M240 60L240 150"/><path class="s" d="M167 101L193 101"/><path class="s" d="M174 109L186 109"/><circle class="s bgf" cx="240" cy="105" r="11"/><path class="s" d="M233.2 98.2L246.8 111.8"/><path class="s" d="M246.8 98.2L233.2 111.8"/><circle class="s bgf" cx="300" cy="105" r="11"/><path class="s" d="M293.2 98.2L306.8 111.8"/><path class="s" d="M306.8 98.2L293.2 111.8"/></g><text class="a" x="80" y="34" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:22px">series</text><text class="" x="80" y="172" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">one shared path</text><text class="a" x="240" y="34" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:22px">parallel</text><text class="" x="240" y="172" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">a path each</text></svg>

cards.title: Your house is wired in parallel
cards.text:
Every socket and light hangs between the live (L) and neutral (N) conductors. That's why each appliance gets the full 230 V, and why switching off the kettle doesn't turn off the fridge.

The more you plug in, the more total current flows in the live wire. That total is what breakers watch.

cards.title: Power
cards.text: Power (watts) is how fast energy is used. Multiply the voltage by the current. Rearranged, I = P ÷ V tells you how much current an appliance draws.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><path class="s bgf" d="M110 150 L120 70 H190 L200 150 Z"/><path class="s" d="M130 62L180 62"/><path class="s" d="M190 82 C232 82 232 140 197 140"/><path class="s" d="M120 92 L96 76 L101 70"/><rect class="s" x="100" y="150" width="110" height="9" rx="3"/><path class="a" d="M145 52 c-6 -8 6 -14 0 -22"/><path class="a" d="M165 52 c-6 -8 6 -14 0 -22"/></g><text class="r" x="275" y="82" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:22px">2300 W</text><text class="" x="275" y="110" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:20px">÷ 230 V</text><text class="a" x="275" y="140" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:24px">= 10 A</text></svg>

cards.title: Breakers vs. RCDs
cards.text:
A breaker (MCB) protects the cable. If too much current flows, the wire would overheat, so it trips. A 16 A breaker on a socket circuit is typical.

An RCD protects people. It compares the current going out on live with the current coming back on neutral. If about 30 mA is missing, it has leaked somewhere, maybe through a person, and it trips in a fraction of a second.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><path class="r" d="M20 70L270 70"/><path class="s" d="M20 110L270 110"/><ellipse class="s" cx="150" cy="90" rx="16" ry="42"/><rect class="s bgf" x="270" y="58" width="36" height="64" rx="3"/><path class="r" d="M40 56L100 56"/><path class="r" d="M92.8 59.5L100 56L92.8 52.5"/><path class="a" d="M110 124L40 124"/><path class="a" d="M47.2 120.5L40 124L47.2 127.5"/></g><text class="r" x="70" y="46" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">10.00 A out</text><text class="" x="75" y="142" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">9.97 A back</text><text class="" x="288" y="95" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">load</text><text class="r" x="200" y="170" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:18px">30 mA missing → trip!</text></svg>

cards.title: Reading your bill: kWh
cards.text: You pay for energy, not power. Energy = power × time, measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh). One kWh is 1 kW running for one hour.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><rect class="s" x="60" y="38" width="200" height="104" rx="8"/><rect class="s bgf" x="80" y="62" width="160" height="38" rx="3"/><circle class="a" cx="160" cy="122" r="6"/></g><text class="mono" x="160" y="89" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:20px">0 1 2 4 6.8</text><text class="a" x="230" y="128" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:18px">kWh</text><text class="" x="160" y="170" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:17px">energy = power × time</text></svg>

quiz.q: Why does each socket in a house get the full 230 V?
options: Each socket has its own transformer
quiz.explain: In parallel, every load sits directly between live and neutral, so each sees the full supply voltage.

quiz.q: A 1150 W heater runs on 230 V. How much current does it draw?

options: Current going out on live doesn't all return on neutral
quiz.explain: An RCD measures the imbalance between live and neutral. Overcurrent is the breaker's job.

quiz.q: A 1.5 kW oven runs for 4 hours. How much energy is that?
